📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Throughout their storied history, the Grand Theft Auto games have usually allowed players to skip the stuff they don't like by using cheat codes. There have been codes to inflate in-game wallets, unlock every gun, and even spawn the best vehicles out of thin air. This time, GTA 6 cheat codes take the franchise in a new direction.

Developer Rockstar Games has, by all accounts, created a GTA game that's at least trying to be a little more serious, sincere, and heartfelt than its predecessors. As such, you cannot simply bust out the "all guns" cheat from the start of the game and go on a rampage. According to PC Gamer, the game does have cheats, but they are only accessible after completing all 91 main story missions.

6 Yes, you have to roll credits on the story to use the GTA 6 cheats. Don't get mad at us, get mad at Rockstar.

PC Gamer confirmed that these cheats can't be used in an early-game save, and activating them will prevent the player from saving from that point on.

According to recent reports, what's even more interesting: Beating the game doesn't immediately let you use the cheats in question; it merely lets you see a list of them, each with a corresponding in-game challenge that needs to be completed before they can be used. Once a cheat is unlocked, it can then be activated by opening the in-game phone, holding L1 and pressing R1 (or LB and RB on Xbox), and then inputting specific button combos.

For example, the "max ammo" cheat (which presumably just fills up all of your guns) requires the player to win 20 bronze medals or better at shooting ranges. If you want infinite ammo, you'll have to win 25 silver medals or better. To access every explosive weapon, you need to throw 100 grenades.

Each cheat's corresponding in-game challenge is related to what the cheat does, which is a very different approach from how they've worked in the past. You can't say Rockstar isn't trying new things.

So, while you can find lists of cheat codes online, they won't do you any good until you beat the game — at which point you'll get the full list.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Vitor Matos was under contract at Swansea until 2030.

Strasbourg have revealed the appointment of Swansea City's Vitor Matos as the club's latest head coach.

The French top-flight side made the announcement on Wednesday evening, but there has been no confirmation of Matos' departure from the Swans.

Strasbourg are expected to pay Swansea compensation thought to be in the region of Â£5m in order to secure his services.

Matos, 38, spent just under a year at Swansea having left his role at Maritimo to succeed Alan Sheehan as the Championship club's head coach in November 2025.

Four members of Matos' coaching team - Diogo Medeiros, Toze Mendes, Goncalo Ricca and head of goalkeeping Pedro Pereira - are also expected to leave Swansea.

Ex-captain Ashley Williams is set to return to the club to join an interim coaching team also featuring fellow former players Kristian O'Leary and Leon Britton.

O'Leary and Britton are set to be the only remaining members of Matos' Swansea staff.

Alongside Williams, they will lead Swansea while the club searches for Matos' permanent successor.

Their first game will be at home to West Bromwich Albion on Saturday.

Swansea go to Middlesbrough next Tuesday before hosting rivals Cardiff City on Sunday, 29 November.

Matos moves on despite agreeing an extended Swansea contract running until 2030 in July.

Leon Britton (left) and Ashley Williams (right) were Swansea team-mates in League One, the Championship and the Premier League.

Swansea were 20th in the second tier when the former Liverpool coach took over, but he leaves a team lying only three points off the top of the table in sixth.

Matos led Swansea to an 11th-placed finish last season, and has raised hopes of a potential promotion push in 2026-27 thanks to an encouraging start to this campaign.

But he told Swansea he wanted to move on after Strasbourg, who have the same ownership group as Premier League side Chelsea, made their move last weekend and he said goodbye to players and staff on Tuesday.

Having finished eighth last season, Strasbourg are 13th in Ligue 1 having won only three of their 10 league games under Hugo Oliveira, who was only appointed in the summer after Gary O'Neil departed to take over at Ipswich Town.

Latest Swansea City news, analysis and fan views.

Listen to the latest Swansea City interviews, news and discussion on BBC Sounds.

Matos was touted as a contender to take charge at Crystal Palace earlier this season - the Eagles have since appointed Thomas Frank - while he had also been linked with a return to Portugal on the back of his impact at Swansea.

When asked in October about the Palace links, Matos said: "I'm Swansea manager. I love being here, love my players, love the staff, so my focus is always on the next game and what we can do better.".

In an interview last week, Swansea chief executive Tom Gorringe acknowledged that Matos' impact will not have gone unnoticed at other clubs.

But Gorringe played down the idea of Matos being lured away, saying: "The reality is there'll always be interest in anyone performing well in any role on and off the pitch.

"That's one of the outcomes of being successful - we're aware of that.

"[But] we're all quite happy. We've all agreed to go on this journey together and we hope that Vitor is here a long time.".

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Shares in the artificial intelligence firm Anthropic began trading on the Nasdaq Global Select Market on Thursday, in the biggest initial public offering of all time.Credit: Idrees Mohammed/AFP via Getty.
  • Sources indicate that anthropic, the frontier artificial-intelligence manufacturer, has made history with the largest initial public offering (IPO) on record on 19 November.
  • Recent findings suggest that the maker of AI model Claude, Anthropic was founded in 2021 by a group who broke away from rival giant OpenAI.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Shares in the artificial intelligence firm Anthropic began trading on the Nasdaq Global Select Market on Thursday, in the biggest initial public offering of all time.Credit: Idrees Mohammed/AFP via Getty.

Sources indicate that anthropic, the frontier artificial-intelligence manufacturer, has made history with the largest initial public offering (IPO) on record on 19 November. With a staggering valuation of around US$1.5 trillion, the firm, based in San Francisco, California, is now among the world’s most valuable companies — and it has major ambitions in science.

Recent findings suggest that the maker of AI model Claude, Anthropic was founded in 2021 by a group who broke away from rival giant OpenAI. Its models have proven powerful in research, and Anthropic has debuted its own directed science effort, focusing on areas including quantum mechanics and protein design. This year alone, it has reported mathematics breakthroughs and launched its first life sciences laboratory.

It has been revealed that the IPO might also unleash a historic wave of philanthropy: all seven of Anthropic’s founders are likely to become billionaires and have pledged to donate 80% of their equity in the company to charity, including chief executive Dario Amodei. And on 18 October, the company declared that it had established the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, created to support initiatives that benefit society and stocked with an initial commitment of 5% of Anthropic’s shares.

But the firm has drawn criticism from researchers, who say its aims of curing diseases on short timescales are unrealistic and that its race towards developing ultra-powerful, ‘superintelligent’ AI models pose serious risks, including an existential threat to humanity. In its public prospectus, published ahead of the IPO, Anthropic outlines a fresh governance structure that it indicates is “consistent with our commitment to AI safety and responsibility”, and adds that safety research directly shapes the firm’s “model design, training, and deployment.”.

Nature looks at four areas of science where Anthropic is making waves.

AI’s potential to turbocharge the discovery of fresh medicines has been a centerpiece of Anthropic’s pitch to investors. “If today we look at things like cancer, Alzheimer’s, heart disease, mental illness — these will be relics of the past in, I think, less than a decade,” Amodei stated in a promotional video ahead of the IPO.

Recent findings suggest that the company has been rapidly expanding its biomedical ambitions. This year, Anthropic opened its first ‘wet’ laboratory for life sciences research, announced partnerships with several pharmaceutical companies, and stated it was pursuing drug leads of its own. “We proposal to scale this work up substantially from here,” the company said on 27 October.

Anthropic bought a one-person, AI-powered biotech: is this drug discovery’s future?

Anthropic bought a one-person, AI-powered biotech: is this drug discovery’s future?

But Amodei’s habit of promising swift, AI-fueled cures for complex diseases has rankled many researchers and entrepreneurs in the field who feel the timeline is unrealistic.

According to recent reports, over the last year, Anthropic has made a major push in the life sciences. In June, the company hired John Jumper, who shared the 2024 Chemistry Nobel Prize for his work on AlphaFold2 while at Google DeepMind in London.

In a recent development, some of the company’s early biological research received a mixed reception from biologists. After Anthropic reported using a swarm of AI agents to find signs of a upcoming CRISPR-like system in viral sequence data, some researchers questioned the novelty of the finding and noted that the company had not carried out the experimental work needed to determine the system’s function.

Recent findings suggest that in protein design — a field that has boomed thanks to specialist AI tools including AlphaFold — Anthropic’s work has also failed to generate much excitement. In August, Anthropic used Claude Science — an agentic system that can access other biological tools and databases — to make novel ‘binders’ against 15 protein targets.

In a recent development, “Expectations are sky high,” notes Anthony Gitter, a computational biologist at the Morgridge Institute for Research in Madison, Wisconsin. “I understand why some view their initial public results as underwhelming.”.

In a recent development, but Gitter is enthusiastic about Anthropic’s protein design efforts, largely because the tech giant was transparent about the work, from the prompts it used to the sequences that were generated. “I would strongly encourage Anthropic to continue that in their future life sciences research,” Gitter adds.

In recent months, Anthropic and other companies — notably Google DeepMind and OpenAI — have been working to establish their research credentials in large part by showing off the rapidly growing mathematical abilities of their flagship AI models.

Recent findings suggest that on 7 September Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge and collaborator Tristan Buckmaster at Newly introduced York University solved a special case of the Navier-Stokes equations, a long-standing problem in mathematical physics that describes the flow of fluids. Hours after Anthropic unveiled the result, OpenAI claimed a full solution of the problem, igniting a controversy.

In another collaboration, Alpöge and mathematical physicist Ethan Sussman at Northwestern University in Evanston, Illinois, have been working towards establishing the mathematical foundations of the standard model of particle physics. This too is a problem on which OpenAI has made similar claims.

In a recent development, anthropic and its competitors see the ability to write a rigorous proof of a mathematical fact as a crucial testing ground for their reasoning models. That’s in large part because the correctness of a proof is an objective measure that can be used as a ‘reward’ to further train AI systems.

Mauricio Pochettino stated it was “an honour” and “a privilege” to be the latest Manchester United head coach after arriving in England on Wednesday.

Pochettino flew from Cincinnati to Manchester overnight after overseeing the USA beating Haiti in his final game in charge. Members of Pochettino’s staff landed earlier in the week to begin work at Carrington, laying the foundations as United seek to turn their season around. His right-hand man, Jesús Pérez, the goalkeeping coach Toni Jiménez and the fitness coach Sebastiano Pochettino, who continues to work with his father, have already taken training with those not on international duty.

Sources indicate that those away with their national teams will return to the club on Thursday, when they are expected to meet Pochettino for the first time and hold meetings. Conversations have also been held with various departments within the club, as Pochettino sought to learn about the squad’s health as he seeks areas of improvement.

Pochettino’s first challenge will be at Anfield on Sunday, when 18th-placed United take on Liverpool. The 54-year-old has his eyes set on rattling Manchester City after being told on TNT Sports that “Manchester’s blue and always will be blue” by DaMarcus Beasley, who once had a loan spell with City. Pochettino responded: “No way. You will see. Give me time … give me time and that is going to start to change.”.

Industry observers note that speaking about joining United, Pochettino stated: “It’s a substantial challenge but at the same time, it’s adrenaline that you want to feel because I think we are going to have a different job. But I think one of the things that is crucial is that we have the experience to deal with that, and I think we need to add our common sense and the way we are going to approach all the things.

Industry observers note that “We know that the situation is not a situation that a club like Manchester United deserves,” Pochettino added. “The fanbase is amazing and after we signed here in America, of every 10 people I crossed in the street, nine are Manchester United fans. It’s amazing.”.

Pochettino is also reunited with the strength and conditioning coach Silvia Tuya, the analyst Alec Scott and his long-term assistant, Miki D’Agostino, at Old Trafford.

After years of anticipation, Grand Theft Auto VI is finally here, and millions of people are experiencing their first hours in Vice City the same way: through someone else's livestream.

According to preliminary data from streaming analytics platform Streams Charts, GTA VI reached 6.38 million concurrent viewers across livestreaming platforms as of 12:30 UTC on Nov. 18. That's roughly 3.7 times the previous game-launch record held by Valorant, whose 2020 closed beta attracted 1.74 million concurrent viewers.

YouTube accounted for 2.66 million viewers, followed by Twitch with 2.50 million and Kick with 1.31 million. On Twitch alone, GTA VI has already surpassed every previous game launch tracked by Streams Charts, becoming the platform's sixth-biggest game category in history.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • BC Game has been the main shirt sponsor of Leicester City for two and a half years.
  • Leicester City have parted ways with their main shirt sponsor after the gambling firm appointed a porn actress as an ambassador.
  • BC Game - which was named as a sponsor for the League One side at the start of the 2024-25 season - named Eva Elfie as a brand ambassador earlier this month.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

BC Game has been the main shirt sponsor of Leicester City for two and a half years.

Leicester City have parted ways with their main shirt sponsor after the gambling firm appointed a porn actress as an ambassador.

BC Game - which was named as a sponsor for the League One side at the start of the 2024-25 season - named Eva Elfie as a brand ambassador earlier this month.

The online gambling company posted a video of Elfie and a delivery driver on social media, with the caption: "Welcome to BC Game Eva Elfie! Let the fun begin.".

The club, which had faced criticism from fans' group The Foxes Trust, remarked it had reached a "mutual agreement" to end its partnership with the firm, and supporters who had bought shirts in the past 28 days could exchange them.

Announcing the club's partnership in 2024, Leicester City said BC Game - which is not available to customers in the UK - was a "socially responsible platform" and aimed to provide an "enjoyable and safe gaming experience".

When Elfie was confirmed as BC Game's brand ambassador, the firm - in a post on LinkedIn on 3 November - noted she had an "established presence in gaming communities".

Chief executive Ali "Ako" Muhanned previously added: "Eva has built an incredible relationship with the gaming and esports community through genuine passion and consistent content creation.".

In response, The Foxes Trust said: "Both gambling and pornography can have devastating impacts on people's lives, in particular young people.

According to recent reports, "Partnerships like these bring these two worlds to a larger audience and, by association, link them to Leicester City. Is this who we are now?".

On Wednesday the club issued a statement, which noted it and the sponsor had "reached a mutual agreement to conclude our commercial partnership with immediate effect".

It also thanked the firm for the "constructive approach taken in reaching this agreement".

The statement confirmed an "enhanced returns policy" in which it would accept BC Game-branded shirts bought since 21 October for exchange or refund, even if they had been worn or personalised.

The firm posted a video announcing its partnership with Eva Elfie on social media.

The Foxes Trust stated it welcomed the decision.

"Since the partnership was declared in 2024, the trust has consistently made clear that BC Game, for numerous reasons, does not reflect the values of our club or its supporters," a spokesperson said.

"That view has been shared by the great majority of fans who responded to our surveys. The recent partnership with an adult content creator only deepened those concerns and the trust felt the need to once again speak out publicly.

According to recent reports, "This statement gained strong traction, emphasising the weight of feeling on this matter. Although we believe that the club should never have gone into partnership with BC Game, we nevertheless welcome this decision to part ways.".

A spokesperson for BC Game added: "BC Game confirms that its principal partner sponsorship agreement with Leicester City Football Club has ended.

"We thank Leicester City for the partnership and wish the club and its supporters all the best for the future.".

Could there be an ancient alien satellite in Earth's orbit? How the 'Black Knight' conspiracy theory has survived for over 100 years

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1541 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In the final days of 1998, as astronauts aboard NASA's Space Shuttle Endeavor were working during one of the early missions to assemble the International Space Station, crew members from the STS-88 mission captured photographs of a dark colored, unusually shaped object drifting through space.
  • In a recent development, despite its unusual appearance in the photographs, the object had a conventional explanation, and one that was known to the astronauts at that time: it was one of several thermal covers that had been wrapped around trunnion pins used in the space station's construction.
  • According to recent reports, seeing the cover drifting away, a frustrated Ross snapped a photograph of it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the final days of 1998, as astronauts aboard NASA's Space Shuttle Endeavor were working during one of the early missions to assemble the International Space Station, crew members from the STS-88 mission captured photographs of a dark colored, unusually shaped object drifting through space.

In a recent development, despite its unusual appearance in the photographs, the object had a conventional explanation, and one that was known to the astronauts at that time: it was one of several thermal covers that had been wrapped around trunnion pins used in the space station's construction. Upon noticing the "escape" of one of the covers, Mission Commander Bob Cabana remarked over the radio to fellow astronaut Jerry Ross that "one of the thermal covers got away from you.".

According to recent reports, seeing the cover drifting away, a frustrated Ross snapped a photograph of it. Yet despite the innocuous story behind the images, they have nonetheless helped fuel belief in an unusual Space Age conspiracy theory: one involving the alleged presence of an ancient satellite, presumably of alien origin, that has long been orbiting our planet — perhaps since the end of the last Ice Age.

According to proponents of this theory, the object photographed by Ross in 1998 is actually what many call the "Black Knight Satellite," and is only one piece of evidence they point to in a long succession of unrelated — and often misinterpreted — events in modern history that supposedly lend further evidence to the alleged alien spacecraft's existence.

So how did such a legend gain traction in the first place, with some versions alleging that NASA and the U.S. government have worked to conceal evidence of the alleged space object's existence from the public?

Depending on which version of the story you come across, the strange roots of the Black Knight conspiracy theory might be traced all the way back to the nineteenth century, when the famous inventor Nikola Tesla began detecting unusual electrical signals while conducting radio experiments at his laboratory in Colorado Springs.

According to recent reports, at the time, Tesla considered whether the signals might be communications from intelligent aliens on nearby planets, although the likely source had actually been terrestrial radio interference. Notably, Tesla also never claimed that the emissions might be coming from an object in Earth's orbit; nonetheless, some proponents of the Black Knight Satellite theories have incorporated Tesla's experiments into the mythos, suggesting they may represent some of the earliest detections of a mysterious object lurking near Earth.

According to recent reports, another component that was later incorporated into the Black Knight Satellite mythos came to light in May 1954, when newspaper reports began publicizing author Donald Keyhoe's assertions that the U.S. Air Force had detected at least two unidentified satellites orbiting Earth.

It has been revealed that at the time, Keyhoe claimed that U.S. government scientists at White Sands were reportedly "making an intensive effort to locate and chart the course of the satellites in an attempt to determine what they are and where they came from," as the author was quoted as saying in articles like one that appeared in the St. Louis Post-Dispatch on Friday, May 14, 1954.

However, later in August of that year, U.S. officials apparently concluded these objects were likely to have been meteors that became "satellites of the Earth and were revolving with it 400 to 600 miles out in space," and that Dr. Lincoln LaPaz, one of the preeminent experts on meteors at the time, had "definitely identified the objects as natural rather than man-made," as reported by the Fresh York Times.

Just a few years later in February 1960, a similar story appeared in Time magazine, which this time alleged that the U.S. Navy had spotted an unidentified dark object in orbit that was suspected of being a Soviet reconnaissance satellite. This object was later identified as well, with officials determining it had likely been debris from the American spy satellite Discoverer 8.

Sources indicate that another similar claim suggests that on May 15, 1963, during the Mercury-Atlas 9 mission, NASA astronaut Gordon Cooper allegedly observed an unusual object in space, which some accounts describe as a "glowing green object" that followed his capsule. While it is true that Cooper reported seeing what he characterized as "John’s fireflies," which were a reference to earlier sightings of unusual luminous objects made by astronaut John Glenn during the Mercury-Atlas 6 mission, it was later concluded that the so-called "fireflies" resulted from small bits of ice separating from the spacecraft itself, which present a greenish hue as sunlight reflects off of them (audio of Cooper describing this during the Mercury-Atlas 9 mission can be found here).

Beyond this, however, there is no evidence of Cooper observing any singular object during this mission, either in Cooper's personal records or mission audio and transcripts from the time.

In a recent development, arguably, one of the most extraordinary components of the Black Knight Satellite theory involves its alleged age, which according to some theories places its initial entry into Earth's orbit as far back as 13,000 years ago. But if so, how would anyone know this, and what evidence could support such an idea?

Industry observers note that understanding this bizarre aspect of the Black Knight mythos requires a look back at the theories of Scottish writer Duncan Lunan, which he first proposed in 1973. At that time, Lunan was receiving international attention for his investigation into mysterious long-delayed echoes, proposing that one theory behind the phenomenon could be that they represented signals from Earth that were being rebroadcast from an extraterrestrial probe — an idea that borrowed from theories first proposed by Australian scientist Ronald Bracewell.

According to Lunan's theory, such a hypothetical "Bracewell probe" might have arrived in Earth's vicinity roughly 13,000 years ago after traveling from within a planetary system associated with the star Epsilon Boötis, some 236 light-years away.

Within just a few years, Lunan had withdrawn his conclusions, but this did little to prevent his initial ideas about a 13,000-year-old alien satellite from being incorporated into the growing mythos surrounding the alleged Black Knight Satellite.

That brings us back to what are arguably the most widely circulated images associated with the Black Knight satellite: the famous images from NASA's STS-88 mission taken by astronaut Jerry Ross in December 1998.

According to spaceflight historian James Oberg, the object in Ross's photos could indeed be positively identified as the thermal blanket lost during the mission, especially since he had specifically asked Ross about the incident — and later misinterpretations of his photos as being evidence of an alien spacecraft — during an October 2014 interview.

At that time, Oberg asked Ross whether he had time during the 1998 spacewalk "to gaze at [the thermal cover] and think about how it looked," to which Ross said no, admitting he had been "too pissed at myself to wonder what it looked like!".

When asked what advice he would offer to those who have misinterpreted the object in his photographs for being something more exotic and otherworldly, Ross told Oberg, "If we see something up there we will be the first ones to ask questions and to tell people we saw something we didn't understand.".

"Conspiracy theories are fun for those working on them, but a waste of valuable brain power," Ross added.

But what, specifically, about the idea of an ancient extraterrestrial probe lurking in orbit around our planet makes this far-fetched theory so captivating?

"I think it's because this idea of an alien satellite kicking around in orbit checks so many conspiracy theory boxes," states Amy Shira Teitel, a spaceflight historian who has also tackled the Black Knight satellite theories in the past, and points to other misperceptions about space that have given rise to conspiracy theories over the years.

"People, for some reason, believe space is fake or that every mission is fake because the Van Allen Belts will kill you," Shira Teitel recently told Space in an email, while noting that most missions take place well within safe distances from the inner radiation belt, with notable exceptions that include the Gemini 11 mission, as well as lunar flights.

"People also love UFOs," she adds. "Even skeptics have a little bit of a soft spot for the idea of an alien craft flying by to say hi. I think when you take all these conspiracy threads together, the Black Knight sort of fits perfectly in that intersection!".

Overall, the bizarre story of the Black Knight satellite offers a textbook example of how a collection of unconnected events and speculative interpretations can gradually accumulate into a single narrative over time.

Despite this reality, belief in the existence of a mysterious ancient satellite lurking in orbit will likely persist for years to come, helping ensure its place as one of the most peculiar — and enduring — legends of the Space Age.

In a recent development, micah Hanks is a science reporter and podcaster focusing on space and astronomy, and Editor at TheDebrief.org. Follow him on X @MicahHanks.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

US women’s head coach won Olympics in 2024.

Hayes enjoyed trophy-laden tenure at Chelsea.

The US women’s national team head coach, Emma Hayes, stated she was “confident in the group that is being put together” to select her next counterpart for the men’s team – a group that includes her.

According to recent reports, speaking after announcing her team’s squad for the ­Concacaf championship and World Cup qualifier, Hayes shed light for the first time on her role in searching for Mauricio Pochettino’s replacement after the Argentinian decamped to Manchester United. US Soccer had previously noted Hayes – alongside the federation CEO, JT Batson, the chief operating officer, Dan Helfrich, and Oguchi Onyewu, the vice-president of sporting – would assist with the search.

Industry observers note that “Listen, I’m very embedded into the federation, and I work really closely with JT, in particular, and even more so with Dan as we’re growing to develop the American soccer movement,” Hayes said. “And you know, JT asked if I would be involved as a technical voice to be involved with the process. And I feel confident in the group of people that have been put together to create a thorough process to select the next men’s national team coach – my role is merely to support that through a technical lens, knowing I do this job … albeit with the women’s team, and that I’ve coached for a number of years, and can offer some of that insight into the application of what to look for and why.”.

Sources indicate that hayes résumé spans 25 years and is distinguished, having coached at the very highest level for club and country alike. The Englishwoman, who took over the US team in 2024, moved from being the assistant coach at Arsenal to taking charge of the Chicago Red Stars in Women’s Professional Soccer in 2008, and later moved to Chelsea, winning the Women’s Super League seven times. Since accepting the US job, she has guided the women to an Olympic gold medal and taken on an expansive role at the federation as it looks to overhaul and grow the women’s game.

“I think it will be a very thorough process,” Hayes said. “I think that’s the most vital part of it. I feel very embedded in what we’re doing with the federation, so it doesn’t feel unusual to me [to help with the search]. So, like I’ve said many times, let’s build off the good work that Mauricio has done. I think that’s the important part, and let’s get it right.”.

In a recent development, hayes offered a heartfelt goodbye to Pochettino on the TNT broadcast of the his final match with the USMNT on Tuesday night, a 2-0 victory over Haiti in their Concacaf Nations League quarter-final. “I just want to say thank you on behalf of all of us at US Soccer, it’s been a privilege to work with you here, see the amazing work you’ve done with the team,” she stated. “I think you’ve left an amazing foundation for someone to come in and build on that great work and the good feeling and certainly the good habits you’ve left with the team. You’ve left a lasting impression on the American people.

Pochettino replied on the broadcast, saying: “I admire a lot Emma. She is a wonderful coach, and a wonderful person. It was an honor to share [this experience] with her.”.

Breaking: Iranian activist and Nobel Peace Prize winner Narges Mohammadi shares her story in memoir

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As PEN International marks Imprisoned Writer Day on November 15, a memoir by 2023 Nobel Peace Prize laureate Narges Mohammadi stands as a powerful act of resistance against authoritarian regimes.

"A Woman Never Stops Fighting — My Struggle for Freedom, Democracy and Human Rights in Iran," was recently published in German and is set to be released in English in September 2027.

The autobiography "portrays how Narges actually became the woman she is today — and it also reveals the price she had to pay to become that woman," Mariam Claren, spokesperson for the Narges Mohammadi Foundation Germany told DW.

It has been revealed that mohammadi wrote the autobiography in prison: "She was constantly writing," notes Claren, whose own mother, activist Nahid Taghavi, shared a cell with Mohammadi for two and a half years, in Iran's notorious Evin prison. "Then, in 2020, Narges was forcibly moved to another prison. All her documents were gone. And she had to start all over.".

But she managed to rewrite it all, and her texts were smuggled out of prison in fragments by fellow prisoners and visitors who risked their own safety.

In her memoir, Mohammadi recounts pivotal moments in her life, including her childhood and youth, how she started taking action against gender discrimination, political repression, the death penalty and human rights abuses, and the personal and emotional toll of her activism.

The human rights activist has been sentenced to a combined total of more than 44 years in prison and 154 lashes. For more than a decade, she has been separated from her twin children, who are now 19 years old and live in exile in France for their own protection.

Born on April 21, 1972, in Zanjan, Iran, Narges Mohammadi became politically active while studying in physics at Imam Khomeini University of Qazvin in the 1990s.

In "A Woman Never Stops Fighting," she describes how she started mountain climbing as a student, and organized mixed-gender groups dedicated to mountaineering — a controversial initiative at the time. She also helped establish an independent student organization and advocated for political reform. Her activities led to repeated harassment and arrests by authorities.

It has been revealed that she began her journalism career in 1996, writing about Iran's student and women's movements. As her public profile grew, she became increasingly involved in Iran's civil society and human rights community.

According to recent reports, in 1998, she married political activist Taghi Rahmani. The couple's twins, Ali and Kiana, were born in 2006.

Over the course of her career, Mohammadi worked with some of Iran's most prominent human rights organizations and became a leading figure in the Defenders of Human Rights Centre, founded by 2003 Nobel Peace Prize laureate Shirin Ebadi.

According to recent reports, she played a key role in initiatives promoting free elections, peace and the abolition of the death penalty, especially for juvenile offenders. She also helped establish organizations supporting political prisoners and advocating for women's rights.

Sources indicate that her first major prison sentence related to her human rights activities came in 2011. It marked the beginning of a cycle of arrests and prosecutions that would define much of her adult life.

In her memoir, she describes an arrest that took place in front of her young children. At one point during her imprisonment, she lost the right to call them for several months.

She also details the brutal treatment she experienced in prison, with constant interrogations, beatings and denial of medical care.

Another central focus of her activism is denouncing the psychological effects of solitary confinement, which she had previously documented with fellow inmates in her book and documentary project "White Torture.".

Sources indicate that "When someone is subjected to physical torture, the scars, blood and infections — dreadful as they may be — serve as visible witnesses," she writes in her memoir. But, she adds, "when someone is subjected to psychological torture, no visible traces remain, and the victim cannot justify the trauma — neither to themselves nor to others. In fact, it becomes virtually impossible to even accept that one has been tortured at all, which causes the suffering to continue indefinitely.".

"This is also the goal of solitary confinement: to bring the imprisoned person to the very edge of nothingness — to strip them of their identity and of everything that makes them human," she writes.

Through her relentless campaigning against executions and state violence, she helped bring these issues to the forefront of public debate among Iranian activists.

International recognition of her work culminated in October 2023 when she was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for "for her fight against the oppression of women in Iran and her fight to promote human rights and freedom for all.".

As Mohammadi was unable to attend the ceremony because she remained imprisoned in Tehran's Evin Prison, the award was accepted on her behalf by her teenage twins, who delivered her message to the world.

Following the Nobel Prize, Iranian authorities continued to pursue new legal cases against her, restrict her communications and intensify pressure on her from prison.

She became the target of a systematic smear campaign, including widespread defamation, gender-based harassment and explicit death threats.

"We are firmly convinced that the Islamic Republic of Iran has deployed its cyber army — which is the second-largest, after Russia's — to this end," states Claren of the Narges Mohammadi Foundation. Conspiracy theorists even started claiming she might be working for the regime, she adds: "And what is truly terrible about this is that when a lie is repeated over and over again and spread over the course of years, it eventually leads even ordinary people to start believing it.".

In late 2024, following surgery, Mohammadi was granted a temporary medical release. Doctors warned at the time that a return to prison could seriously endanger her health.

Nevertheless, Mohammadi was brutally arrested again in December 2025, while attending a memorial ceremony for Khosrow Alikordi, a lawyer and human rights activist who died in suspicious circumstances.

Recent findings suggest that in prison, she was held in solitary confinement for an extended period and her health continued to deteriorate, Claren reports. But "thanks to a public campaign, she has now been granted what is known as an interruption of detention for medical reasons.".

But "that doesn't mean she is free," adds Claren, who notes that she still suffers from serious health problems — as do many Iranians who have been tortured in prison.

In February, an Iranian court ordered additional prison sentences for Mohammadi, along with a travel ban.

Mohammadi lives in constant fear of having to return to prison any day, notes Claren, and "this all comes with the pressure to which Iranian civil society — including, of course, people like Narges — is at the moment subjected, with questions like: Will Trump launch an attack, yes or no? Will there be another war?".

Despite this uncertainty, Mohammadi continues her activism. Her international profile also helps her supporters keep addressing publicly the issue of human rights in Iran in the public eye, claims Claren: "It is incredibly important that, alongside the individual Narges Mohammadi, the focus also remains consistently on the struggle of the people in Iran for freedom, dignity, and fundamental rights — for the right to sing and dance.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Simone Magill's return is a significant boost for Michael McArdle's side.

Northern Ireland manager Michael McArdle has made five changes to his squad for the upcoming friendlies against Greece, with the return of experienced striker Simone Magill among the notable returnees.

Magill, who gave birth to her daughter Skye over the summer, returned to training with the Northern Ireland squad last month but did not play in either leg of the World Cup play-off defeat by Portugal.

The 32-year-old Birmingham City forward has not represented Northern Ireland since announcing her pregnancy just over a year ago and will now be hoping to add to her 95 caps and 28 international goals.

According to recent reports, glentoran midfielder Chloe McCarron returns after an injury-hit spell, while Hibernian's Joely Andrews is also back after missing the Portugal games through injury. Both featured for Northern Ireland at the Euros in 2022.

Kerry Beattie completes the trio of returnees in the 24-player squad after impressing in front of goal since joining Portsmouth from Aberdeen during the summer.

'You can be a mum and a footballer - they can co-exist'.

Family, football and Dalglish - what drives NI boss McArdle?

In a recent development, there is also a senior recall for defender Ella Haughey. The 22-year-old West Brom player last received a call-up in 2021, when she was named among the substitutes for friendlies against England and Scotland.

Meanwhile, Kess Elmore, Jane McMaster and Lucy-Jayne Grant have retained their places after receiving their first senior call-ups last month.

Injured defender Natalie Johnson misses out, alongside Mia Moore, Naomi McLaughlin, Charlotte Havern and Leyla McFarland.

Both matches will take place at Inver Park in Larne, with the first meeting scheduled for Friday 27 November before the sides face off again on Tuesday 1 December.

Northern Ireland currently sit 52nd in the Fifa world rankings, six places above Greece.

The Birmingham City forward's return has been carefully managed through close collaboration between Northern Ireland and her club, with both parties keen to ensure she is given the time and support needed to make the transition back into competitive football.

Michael McArdle was delighted to welcome his captain back into the fold, revealing that Magill's family were also involved in the previous international camp as she began preparing for life as a mother and professional footballer.

"I'm delighted we've got our captain back," McArdle told BBC Sport NI.

"We've had on the last camp Simone, her husband Mark and Skye as well, just as a transition for us all to get ready for the future for Simone as a mother athlete now.

"That's the exciting piece for her, but great to have her back in a playing capacity now. No pressure or expectation for Simone. It's part of the process collaboratively between us and Birmingham.".

Magill also had the opportunity to get back on the training pitch during the previous camp, taking another important step in her gradual return.

McArdle explained that considerable work has been taking place behind the scenes at Birmingham City, with the club's performance staff working closely alongside Northern Ireland's team to manage her progress.

"There's a lot of work going on at the club just now to support Simone's return," he mentioned.

"This opportunity to be in camp and selected again is that opportunity to take that, hopefully playing minutes as well.".

Although she has yet to make a public appearance for Birmingham this season, McArdle confirmed that Magill has continued working and gaining minutes behind closed doors.

"We've been very close with Birmingham since pre-season, so Birmingham's performance team and our performance team work together," he added.

Recent findings suggest that for Northern Ireland, however, her return is about more than simply adding another player to the squad. Magill's experience, leadership and influence remain hugely key.

"Her presence, obviously, is our captain and our leader within the playing group, for us as staff as well," McArdle said.

With no expectations placed on her immediate playing involvement, the priority is ensuring Magill's comeback happens at the right pace, while allowing Northern Ireland to benefit from having their captain back among the group.

Goalkeepers: Jackie Burns (Burnley), Lauren Perry (Montrose), Maddy Harvey-Clifford (Cliftonville).

Defenders: Rebecca Holloway and Rebecca McKenna (both Birmingham City), Abi Sweetlove and Jane McMaster (both Linfield), Ellie Mason (Charlton), Fi Morgan (Celtic), Ella Haughey (West Bromwich Albion), Lucy-Jayne Grant (Galway United).

Midfielders: Chloe McCarron and Aimee Kerr (both Glentoran), Joely Andrews (Hibernian), Brenna McPartlan (Burnley), Connie Scofield (Sheffield United), Emily Cassap (Sunderland).

Forwards: Lauren Wade and Keri Halliday (both Hearts), Simone Magill (Birmingham City), Casey Howe (Celtic), Kerry Beattie (Portsmouth), Cora Chambers (Linfield), Kess Elmore (Sparta Prague).

💡 Key Takeaways
  • YouTube is making another significant change to how views are counted on long-form videos, YouTube Shorts, and livestreams.
  • According to a tech giant patch, YouTube will now include "co-views" in public video view counts.
  • It's YouTube's estimate of how many people are watching content together on TV via a single account.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

YouTube is making another significant change to how views are counted on long-form videos, YouTube Shorts, and livestreams.

According to a tech giant patch, YouTube will now include "co-views" in public video view counts.

It's YouTube's estimate of how many people are watching content together on TV via a single account.

YouTube says it will include these estimated views because "viewers are now watching over 1 billion hours of YouTube on TVs every day." The firm says it wants to "credit creators true reach" and "provide a more complete picture of how audiences are engaging with content.".

Recent findings suggest that this isn't the first recent change to how YouTube counts video views. This past summer, the platform started counting views from the moment a video plays. Previously, viewers had to watch for a specific amount of time, typically around 30 seconds for long-form videos, in order for their view to be counted in the public metric. The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile.

Co-views is certainly a bit more offbeat than that, as the organization is essentially inflating view counts by estimating how many people are watching together on a single device that would've previously been counted as a single view.

YouTube, however, says this new platform metric "aligns with TV industry standards, including how traditional broadcast and streaming networks estimate the total number of people exposed to content.".

The tech giant indicates it is using a statistical model that utilizes "factors like demographic patterns and viewing times.".

Creators will be able to see new co-view rate analytics in YouTube Studio to gauge how this metric affects their overall views.

This new metric will only be applied to video views on TV, so if users watch content with friends and family on their desktop or mobile device, co-views won't be counted. YouTube will only count co-views going forward and will not retroactively apply them to videos on the platform.

The Leonid meteor shower peaks tonight! Here's what you need to know

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (539 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the Leonid meteor shower peaks tonight (Nov.
  • Sources indicate that up to 15 meteors could be spotted per hour under perfect dark sky conditions on the night of Nov.
  • In a recent development, leonid meteors appear to race away from a point of origin, or radiant, in the constellation Leo, which glistens high above the southeastern horizon in the hours before dawn in mid-November.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the Leonid meteor shower peaks tonight (Nov. 17-18) sending shooting stars and fireballs across the autumn sky as Earth passes through a stream of debris left by Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle.

Sources indicate that up to 15 meteors could be spotted per hour under perfect dark sky conditions on the night of Nov. 17-18, according to the International Meteor Organisation. NASA, meanwhile, has given a more conservative rate of less than three meteors per hour — time will tell.

In a recent development, leonid meteors appear to race away from a point of origin, or radiant, in the constellation Leo, which glistens high above the southeastern horizon in the hours before dawn in mid-November. Both Jupiter and Mars will be separated by just a few degrees in the constellation Leo on the night of the peak, making it particularly easy to find in 2026!

The best time to spot Leonids is in the hours before dawn on Nov. 18, when the radiant will reach its highest point in the southeastern sky, maximizing the amount of meteors that may be seen skimming through Earth's atmosphere. By then, the waxing moon will have set, leaving darker skies and a better chance of spotting fainter meteors.

Shooting stars that appear close to the radiant will strike Earth almost head-on, leaving the shortest trails. Instead, find a patch of sky a short distance away from the constellation Leo, where the meteors will be at their most impressive, and give your eyes 20-30 minutes to fully adapt to the dark.

As if shooting stars weren't enough, the Leonid shower is also known for spawning dazzling fireballs and long-lasting Earth-grazing meteors, which strike our atmosphere at an oblique angle, leaving long trains as they skim through before passing back out into space.

The shower is also capable of producing magnificent meteor storms when Earth passes through particularly dense trails of debris left behind by Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, which orbits the sun approximately every 33 years.

Read more: 'It looked like every star in the sky was falling': Eyewitnesses remember the great Leonid meteor storm of 1966.

Recent findings suggest that sadly, we'll have to wait a bit for the next major show. According to the Planetary Society, another Leonid meteor storm could occur as early as 2031, while a study released in August 2026 predicts potentially spectacular displays in 2033 and 2034.

Want to photograph a shooting star? Then be sure to read our guide to imaging shooting stars, along with our selections of the best lenses and cameras for astrophotography on the market in 2026.

He has a passion for the night sky, science, Hideo Kojima, and human space exploration, and can’t wait for the day when astronauts once again set foot on the moon.

#47766. Joint-record six referee errors in last Premier League weekend

Joint-record six referee errors in last Premier League weekend

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1257 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The failure to award a penalty to Arsenal would have been more controversial had the Gunners not scored a second-half winner.
  • The Premier League's Key Match Incidents Panel has ruled there were six on-field errors in the last round of games - the joint-highest it has recorded in one weekend.
  • Each week, the five members of the panel assess all the contentious incidents and vote whether both the referee and the video assistant referee (VAR) have got the decisions correct.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The failure to award a penalty to Arsenal would have been more controversial had the Gunners not scored a second-half winner.

The Premier League's Key Match Incidents Panel has ruled there were six on-field errors in the last round of games - the joint-highest it has recorded in one weekend.

Each week, the five members of the panel assess all the contentious incidents and vote whether both the referee and the video assistant referee (VAR) have got the decisions correct.

You have to go back to the early part of the 2023-24 season to find the last time there were six mistakes logged.

The statistic does not include correct VAR interventions to fix errors, such as the red card shown to Brentford's Igor Thiago.

In the last round of games almost every fixture had a contentious refereeing situation which was hotly debated.

It started on Friday with a potential penalty to Coventry City for a hair pull by Everton's James Tarkowski.

Arsenal were denied a penalty following a VAR review after it was deemed Kai Havertz was offside.

Tottenham lodged a complaint over a challenge by Leeds United's Jayden Bogle, who was not shown a red card.

And Liverpool argued against a late Crystal Palace penalty.

It has been revealed that but which decisions did the KMI Panel rule were incorrect? Some of the votes might surprise you.

Recent findings suggest that such was the controversy across the weekend, it may come as a surprise that the KMI Panel ruled only two were missed VAR interventions. There have been six missed overall, the same number as this stage last season.

Incident 1: Coventry's Caleb Yirenkyi appeared to have his hair pulled inside the area by Everton's James Tarkowski. No penalty was awarded.

KMI Panel vote: 5:0 incorrect, for the on-field decision and the VAR.

What the KMI Panel said: "Tarkowski had a hold of Yirenkyi's hair and the panel unanimously felt that VAR should have intervened.".

Incident 2: Arsenal's Kai Havertz was pulled down inside the area by Hull City's Nobel Mendy. The VAR, Michael Oliver, sent referee Farai Hallam to the pitchside monitor but it was not given due to an offside offence by the Germany international.

KMI Panel vote: 5:0 incorrect, for the on-field decision and the VAR.

What the KMI Panel said: "Although Harvertz is clearly in an offside position, there is a clear and impactful holding action by Mendy before any potential offside offence.".

Frank Lampard post-match interview - Everton v Coventry.

When the KMI Panel sits down to vote there are two separate considerations.

The first is on the decision of the referee, which is a basic judgement in law and the Premier League's expected interpretation.

Sources indicate that the second is on the potential VAR intervention. This takes into account what the referee has stated, the available replay angles and the high bar for intervention.

Incident 1: Thierno Barry put Everton in front against Coventry in the 61st minute, but there was a VAR check for a potential handball.

KMI Panel vote: 2:3 incorrect on the field, but 5:0 no VAR intervention.

Recent findings suggest that what the KMI Panel said: "On the balance of probability the ball did accidentally strike Barry's hand. However, the readily available footage did not provide conclusive evidence.".

It has been revealed that incident 2: Crystal Palace were awarded a penalty against Liverpool three minutes into stoppage time for a foul by Milos Kerkez on Dario Osorio. But was it just a clash of heads?

KMI Panel vote: 0:5 incorrect on the field, but 5:0 no VAR intervention.

What the KMI Panel mentioned: "A penalty was incorrect with the contact being inevitable. However, it was not a clear and obvious error.".

Incident 3: Ipswich were awarded a 72nd-minute penalty against Bournemouth for a foul by Lewis Cook on Abdoul Ouattara.

KMI Panel vote: 1:4 incorrect on the field, but 4:1 no VAR intervention.

What the KMI Panel mentioned: "Ouattara made a clear step across Cook who didn't make a challenge and the referee's decision to award a penalty was incorrect. However, it was not a clear and obvious error.".

Incident 4: Potential second yellow card for Bournemouth's Marcus Tavernier.

KMI Panel vote: 2:3 incorrect on the field; no VAR intervention possible.

What the KMI Panel mentioned: "There was a clear, deliberate action by Tavernier to delay the restart.".

Some of the most high-profile decisions from across the weekend have not yet featured.

That is because they have been voted to be correct on the field and through VAR.

In a recent development, incident 1: Leeds United's Jayden Bogle caught Tottenham's Mathys Tel on high on his ankle. There was no VAR review for a red card.

KMI Panel vote: 3:2 correct on the field and for the VAR intervention.

In a recent development, what the KMI Panel remarked: "The majority felt Bogle was looking to challenge with his right leg and his left leg came down on the back of Tel's ankle without the speed, force or intensity to be serious foul play. Two panellists felt that the challenge was sufficiently dangerous to merit a red card.".

Incident 2: Chelsea's Cole Palmer went down on the edge of the area under a challenge by Sunderland's Luke O'Nien.

KMI Panel vote: 4:1 correct on the field and for the VAR intervention.

In a recent development, what the KMI Panel noted: "Clear contact made by O'Nien on Palmer which the panel felt should have been penalised with a free-kick on the basis that contact was made outside the area. One panellist felt that the foul contact was inside the area.".

Incident 3: Sunderland were awarded a penalty when Levi Colwill was ruled to have tripped Brian Bobbey.

KMI Panel vote: 5:0 correct on the field and for the VAR intervention.

What the KMI Panel said: "There was upper body holding from both players as they progressed into the penalty area before a careless trip by the Chelsea defender.".

Incident 4: Possible foul by Senne Lammens on Aston Villa goalkeeper Zion Suzuki before Patrick Dorgu's 96th-minute equaliser.

KMI Panel vote: 5:0 correct on the field and for the VAR intervention.

What the KMI Panel said: "Although Lammens turned away from the ball, the contact he made on Suzuki was not impactful.".

The KMI Panel was scrapped this summer in the Scottish Premiership because clubs became frustrated with the voting patterns of its members.

But it is more important in the Premier League, with the results creating a merit table which contributes to 50% of referees' salaries in bonus payments.

Many fans will feel there should have been more than two VAR errors logged in the last round of games.

Yet the KMI Panel does not exist to mirror the opinion of supporters.

Crucially, it uses the laws of the game and how the Premier League expects its games to be refereed as the barometer.

Still, six on-field mistakes - plus the Thiago red card - is clearly a high number.

And fans struggle to understand why it seems to be OK to have these on-field errors, and not correct them due to the high bar.

It all adds to the frustration of VAR.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cryptocurrency casino made Eva Elfie a brand ambassador.

Club end deal early citing ‘differing commercial priorities’.

Leicester City have ditched their front-of-shirt sponsor, BC Game, after the cryptocurrency casino’s partnership with a porn actor sparked a fan backlash. BC Game, an offshore firm registered in Belize that is unlicensed to operate in the UK, had been Leicester’s main sponsor since 2024.

Industry observers note that this month BC Game named Eva Elfie a brand ambassador, leading the Foxes Trust, Leicester’s supporters’ trust, to highlight the “devastating impacts” caused by gambling and pornography. On Wednesday the club said they prematurely ended their agreement with the online betting firm after they “recognised our differing commercial priorities”.

It is understood Leicester directly raised concerns with BC Game about the implications of their deal with Elfie, a Russian porn actor who BC Game noted had “an established presence in gaming communities”. Leicester’s deal with BC Game, which began in July 2024, was due to run until the end of the season.

Industry observers note that the trust had previously outlined concerns about the club’s partnership with BC Game. In a statement responding to the partnership this month, they said: “From the moment the club decided to take sponsorship from a betting firm we felt Leicester City were ditching its values.

“Now throw into the mix that BC Game have entered into a partnership with someone who continues to make their name via adult content. Partnerships like these bring these two worlds to a larger audience and, by association, link them to Leicester City. Is this who we are now?”.

Leicester, who visit Huddersfield in League One on Saturday, mentioned supporters who purchased a shirt featuring BC Game branding within the past 28 days are able to exchange the shirt or are eligible for a full refund. The club added they would pay for the postage of returns via standard delivery.

Leicester remain for sale, with the club’s Thai owners, King Power, also seeking to sell their stadium, training base and women’s team.

In a recent development, in an unrelated development, the former Chelsea technical director Michael Emenalo is working as an adviser to the club, who are 11th in the third tier. Emenalo is among a team of Deloitte consultants Leicester say they have enlisted to “assess its current operations and inform its future strategic planning”.

Industry observers note that the headline news is alarming — malware reportedly made its way to popular websites people visit every day — but the researcher found that the attackers' crypto wallets only contained about $7,000, all of which was transferred during a nine-hour time period on Nov. 16. And just because malware appeared on a site, that doesn't necessarily mean that hackers successfully exploited visitors to that sites. Breaking: Could lack of money sink TFFF rainforest fund before it even launches?

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1087 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The world's tropical forests play a vital role in slowing global heating and preserving biodiversity, storing climate-damaging carbon dioxide and providing a home for an extremely large number of species — when they're intact.
  • More than 140 countries committed to halting global deforestation by the end of the decade at the 2021 UN climate change conference in Glasgow, but five years later logging continues.
  • It has been revealed that in 2024, over 8 million hectares (19 million acres) of forest were lost.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The world's tropical forests play a vital role in slowing global heating and preserving biodiversity, storing climate-damaging carbon dioxide and providing a home for an extremely large number of species — when they're intact.

More than 140 countries committed to halting global deforestation by the end of the decade at the 2021 UN climate change conference in Glasgow, but five years later logging continues.

It has been revealed that in 2024, over 8 million hectares (19 million acres) of forest were lost. And since 1990, nearly 490 million hectares of forest have been wiped out.

It has been revealed that more recently, the trend has shifted in the opposite direction. Deforestation in the Amazon region of Brazil decreased by 41% from August 2025 through 2026 to reach its lowest rate since records began.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

To ensure lasting protection, the Tropical Forest Forever Facility was debuted in 2025 at the COP30 climate conference in Belem, Brazil.

Because rainforests are so important for the world, the idea behind the fund was to give money to the countries where they are located to help them preserve and protect these ecosystems.

So far, these countries have made more profit through deforestation — for example, by mining natural resources on rainforest land or farming the area.

Industry observers note that starting in 2027, the TFFF is expected to generate the funds needed for rainforest conservation, in part via contributions from various countries. By the end of this year, a total of $10 billion (€8.9 billion) in government capital is due to flow into the fund, mainly in the form of low-interest loans.

In addition, the TFFF is expected to issue bonds to private investors, such as banks and investment firms, to raise additional funds — initially totaling about $40 billion.

Recent findings suggest that going forward, the plan is for governments to contribute a total of $25 billion to the pot, and for private donors to contribute $100 billion. The fund will then invest this money in international financial markets with the aim of generating profits.

Private investors who purchase TFFF bonds can expect to earn about 5% interest per bond per year, said Felix Finkbeiner, the founder of the German environmental organization Plant-for-the-Planet, where he is responsible for forest conservation and advocacy.

"Private investors' capital is very well protected," Finkbeiner mentioned, adding that any losses the TFFF might incur on the capital markets — for example, if the price of its bonds should fall — would be offset by government funds.

About 2.7% of the TFFF's profits would be set aside for countries with tropical forests.

Recent findings suggest that countries would receive $4 per year for every hectare of forest that they preserve instead of chopping down. At least 20% of these funds must be allocated to Indigenous peoples and local communities.

According to calculations by the TFFF Watch website, an independent platform debuted by Plant-for-the-Planet to track investments, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, for example, would receive about $333 million for its 2024 forest stock under this system.

Finkbeiner mentioned the subsidies would be paid only for intact ecosystems and not for timber plantations, with forest areas and their condition mapped and assessed using satellite imagery. Though it can sometimes be difficult to identify plantations accurately on satellite photos, he said, the technology has improved significantly over the last decade.

That means any NGO or external party with access to the satellite data can check the condition of the region, providing further oversight. If forest areas are cleared or damaged, money is deducted from the total.

Another safeguard: If countries don't use the TFFF funds for rainforest conservation, their payments could be frozen for the next few years.

The TFFF is supposed to invest, whenever possible, in government bonds issued by emerging and developing countries. Above all, the idea is not to invest in projects that harm the climate — such as those linked to oil, gas, or coal investments.

The TFFF concept has received plenty of support from environmental organizations, in part because it gives countries in the Global South significantly more sovereignty than traditional forms of development financing.

"For example, if the government of Ghana wants to protect its rainforest today, it usually asks the World Bank for financial assistance — and then the World Bank in [Washington] DC decides whether Ghana is allowed to do so," Finkbeiner said.

In a recent development, the TFFF fund is also designed to be immune to donor countries' backing out in the event of a change in government, for example. Once a contribution is made, the money remains in the fund for 40 years before being paid back.

Continuing protection is also an incentive for countries receiving money from the fund. "When a fresh government comes into power that wants to cut back a little on climate protection, they will realize: We'll get more money if we protect the rainforest," mentioned Finkbeiner.

For the rainforest fund to actually get off the ground, a total of $10 billion in seed capital must be raised by the end of 2026. So far, the confirmed pledges from countries, NGOs and foundations total only $7.9 billion.

Eight countries have expressed a willingness to contribute so far, including Brazil, Indonesia, France, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands and Luxembourg.

Sources indicate that norway, with a pledge of $3 billion, is the largest would-be donor. However, the government in Oslo is willing to honor its commitment only if the agreed-upon total amount is in place by the end of the year.

"This deadline isn't set in stone, but otherwise the Norwegian government will have real trouble getting it through parliament," Finkbeiner remarked.

Germany's commitment must also still be approved by the parliament. The German government has pledged about €1 billion to the TFFF starting in 2027, to be paid out over 10 years.

Other countries are also considering investing in the TFFF, including Canada, China, South Korea and the United Arab Emirates.

Philanthropic organizations have pledged $88 million to the fund so far, including $73 million announced this week during the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey. Finkbeiner remains upbeat.

"Promises like that always come at the last minute," he remarked. "I'm very optimistic that we'll secure more commitments at the COP — and in the course of December — and that we'll then reach that $10 billion.".

#47761. Breaking: The 3pm football blackout: Outdated or still relevant in 2026?

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1595 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Co ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: The 3pm football blackout: Outdated or still relevant in 2026?

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1595 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The 3pm blackout has existed in English football since the 1960s.
  • After 60 years, is time finally running out on the 3pm blackout in football?
  • With pretty much every available television slot now exhausted, next year the Premier League and the EFL are set to hold serious discussions about its future.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The 3pm blackout has existed in English football since the 1960s.

After 60 years, is time finally running out on the 3pm blackout in football?

With pretty much every available television slot now exhausted, next year the Premier League and the EFL are set to hold serious discussions about its future.

There are concerns, especially within non-league football, that removing the blackout could have detrimental effects on attendances and finances.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham agrees, urging caution and suggesting the health of the football pyramid should come first.

But many Premier League fans feel they are short-changed, locked out of many of their team's fixtures just because they live in this country.

Go anywhere else in the world, and every single match is available live.

With streaming so prevalent, to some the blackout feels archaic.

Yet it is a complex situation, and many feel the depth of English football's pyramid is like nowhere else.

BBC Sport looks at the history of the blackout, why it is unique to British football and the arguments for and against keeping it.

It is the start of the 1964-65 season and the BBC launches a programme called Match of the Day.

Highlights of one match would be broadcast on BBC Two, a channel which at the time was only available in London.

Yet some clubs were concerned. Would fans still turn up to games?

It has been revealed that burnley chairman Bob Lord was the first owner to refuse to allow the cameras into Turf Moor. At the end of the season, several other clubs tried to block the renewal of the deal.

A compromise was reached and the BBC agreed not to reveal the televised Saturday match until all games had ended.

Shortly afterwards came the blackout for live matches.

Fast forward 20 years to 1987. With dwindling attendances across the European domestic leagues, partly influenced by crowd trouble, Uefa took up England's idea.

Article 48 was added to the Uefa Statutes.

Each country could designate a two-and-a-half-hour "transmission-free period", as long as at least 50% of matches in the top two leagues were taking place.

This was "designed to ensure that spectators are not deterred from attending local football matches of any kind and/or participating in matches at amateur and/or youth level".

Today, the situation has gone full circle. The only leagues that apply Article 48 are England, Scotland and Northern Ireland.

The reason for this is simpler than you might imagine.

No other major country qualifies for the blackout - because no other major country has a kick-off time that runs from the top flight and through the divisions.

It is a tradition that is unique to football in the United Kingdom.

Let's take Germany, often held up as an example of a country with excellent attendances despite not having a blackout.

In a recent development, this misses a key point. The Bundesliga has its own kick-off slot, 3:30pm on a Saturday, and no other division plays at the same time. The 2. Bundesliga, for instance, has a standard Saturday kick-off time of 1:30pm.

Could you imagine English football replicating this?

The other top leagues are the same.

According to recent reports, in Spain, it is rare for either of the top two divisions to have games that kick off simultaneously. Each match has its own slot, and is broadcast live.

In Italy, Serie A plays on a Sunday afternoon, and Serie B on a Saturday.

In France, Ligue 1 has Saturday night as its main time slot, Ligue 2 plays largely on a Friday night, and Ligue 3 on a Saturday lunchtime.

So there is no blackout, because the football calendar works in a completely different way.

Football fans give their thoughts on the Saturday 3pm TV blackout.

The next television rights cycle presents a unique opportunity.

The deals for the Premier League, EFL and Scottish Premiership are all up for renewal in 2029-30.

There is the chance for all the top stakeholders to come together and agree to end the blackout.

Last year, Premier League chief executive Richard Masters noted there were no intends to remove the blackout.

But this summer there was a clear shift in emphasis, with Masters admitting there would be talks with the EFL ahead of the renewal of TV rights.

Scottish football has gone first, with broadcasters invited to bid to show all matches live - and is open to those shown on a Saturday afternoon.

It will be another year before we discover what the Premier League and the EFL - which seriously considered ending the blackout three years ago - are prepared to offer to broadcasters.

So, why would the leagues need to offer up the Saturday 3pm slot to broadcasters? After all, the latest domestic Premier League deal was worth a record Â£6.7bn - an increase of 4%.

According to recent reports, however, to achieve that figure, the Premier League had to make an additional 70 games available. In real terms, it means each live Premier League game is worth less than it was before.

Now every single game not shown at 3pm on a Saturday - and there are only 110 left - is on TV.

Could the Premier League need to offer more matches for the rights to keep their overall value?

If so there are two options: try to find more TV slots, or show games at 3pm on a Saturday.

Could the Women's Super League benefit too? It looked into playing a 3pm on a Saturday but could not find a way around the blackout.

Most of the competition's games are shown live already, with a greater concern being stadium availability and consistency of kick-off times.

There is a danger that the concern of the 3pm blackout is viewed only through the lens of Premier League and EFL television rights.

But it goes much deeper than that.

Tom Greatrex, the chair of the Football Supporters' Association, says there are attendances in non-league football that some top flights in Europe "would look at jealously".

"We have one of the strongest football pyramids in the world, with excellent matchday attendances deep into the non-league game," Greatrex mentioned.

"The prime minister is right to point out the value of the blackout to clubs further down the pyramid, and to urge caution over the impact rushed change could have on the overall health of the game.".

BBC Sport understands that senior executives at the National League, which has a long-term global streaming deal with DAZN, are steadfastly against the blackout ending.

It has serious reservations, shared by the vast majority of its 72 clubs, that attendances would be impacted.

Included in this is transient attendance from season ticket holders of league clubs, many of whom go to non-league football when their team is away from home, boosting receipts considerably.

The fear is this could be lost if all league games are streamed at 3pm.

Nick Boom, the chair of Northern Premier League side FC United of Manchester, worries that the glitch is only viewed through the lens of top-flight football.

"Football doesn't begin and end with the Premier League," Boom told BBC Sport.

"Every Saturday, thousands of people turn out to support their local clubs.

"For many of those clubs, the income from people coming through the turnstiles, buying a pint or something to eat is what keeps them alive.

"The 3pm blackout isn't about nostalgia. It's about protecting something that matters.".

Boom added that clubs in non-league football are huge community assets, and losing them would have an impact "well beyond 90 minutes on a Saturday".

Some clubs are more open-minded about what ending the blackout could mean for non-league football.

Others have changed the way they operate to get around it.

North West Counties League Premier Division side FC Isle of Man have stopped playing at 3:00pm on a Saturday so they can stream all their games live.

Brian Shotton, a director at eighth-tier Ashington FC, told BBC Sport that he would not be automatically against removing the blackout.

"I would still have concerns, because every person through the gate makes a difference," Shotton stated.

"I don't think we should just assume it would damage non-league football, but equally you need to know what it could mean for clubs like ours.".

Ashington, who have attendances of about 400, see gates rise by up to 25% when Newcastle are not at home - but they already feel the impact of illegal streaming of the Magpies' games.

For the official broadcasters like Sky Sports, these supporters are seen as lost revenue.

There is an argument that the blackout drives piracy. Just how many of those particular fans would pay for a legal subscription is open to debate.

Added to that, there are now many weekends when fewer than 50% of matches in the top two divisions are played at 3pm on a Saturday anyway.

For instance, on 28 November there are just two in the Premier League, and seven in the Championship.

Other non-league clubs, like Dorking Wanders and Hashtag United, have spoken of the opportunities ending the blackout could bring, such as more income streams and fewer inconvenient kick-off times.

According to recent reports, but this, for now, seems to be a minority view. The concerns for the health of the entire pyramid, on attendances and finances, are real.

Once the blackout is gone, it is unlikely to come back.
